chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: Students who start at Coltrane and skip the roots
summary: Ted Jr. says Berklee students know post-Coltrane jazz but not Hawkins or the basics.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well, I find -- I'm speaking to Teddy Wilson, Jr., -- I'm saying do you envision that perhaps this will happen, that we can overcome this some day, that this might be the way to expand? What do you think about that?
Well, I can speak for Berklee and I believe that it could be possible, but unfortunately, all the students are too interested in post-Coltrane jazz; Coltrane, mostly Coltrane.
Well, don't you think that's normal? That generation era.

Yeah, but I think that any jazz musician should understand the roots first and then go on to Coltrane, if he wants or wherever else he wants to go; but unfortunately, when they all start at Coltrane, and some of them haven't even heard of Coleman Hawkins. And some of them are pretty decent players, in the jazz field, but they don't know the roots and they have no idea of the basics of jazz. I think it's a serious handicap.
It's beautiful to hear you say that.
I was all the more surprised to

find this at Berklee because Berklee is supposed to be THE jazz school of America, you know; take Northeastern or North Texas University; that is, a university that is not solely a jazz university - but jazz happens to be a branch in there, but Berklee is supposedly the best jazz school in America. And I find that a serious shortcoming.
